title: Ashwagandha
subtitle: The Ayurvedic tonic root: powders, warm milks, and long-course tinctures
excerpt: Ashwagandha is a small shrubby plant whose root has been the central tonic herb of Ayurvedic medicine for over two thousand years. In western home practice, the dried root powder is stirred into warm milk or taken as a tincture over several weeks. A jar of powder keeps 12 months sealed in a cool cupboard.

glossaryTerms.definition: A term used in western herbal practice for herbs traditionally taken over weeks to support the body's response to sustained stress. The concept has Ayurvedic and modern phytotherapy roots.
A herb or preparation taken over a longer period, weeks to months, with the aim of supporting general vitality rather than addressing a single acute symptom.

herbal extract taken over several weeks. The central strengthening herb of Ayurvedic medicine, long prepared as a warming drink for sustained energy and resilience during periods of depletion. A jar of dried root powder keeps 12 months in a cool, dark cupboard.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Withania somnifera, family Solanaceae. A small shrub, 30 to 150 cm, with velvety grey-green leaves and small, unremarkable greenish-yellow flowers. Native to India, North Africa, and the Mediterranean. cultivated widely in India, where the root is harvested from one-to-two-year-old plants in winter. The root is the part used, thick, fleshy, white-to-yellowish inside, with a characteristic horse-like smell (the Sanskrit name means 'smell of horse'). Sold as dried whole root, cut root, or as a brown-grey powder.
The root contains several active compounds: alkaloids, iron, and plant sugars. Western herbal practice and Ayurveda both frame ashwagandha as an
: a herb used over weeks for depletion and stress. Ayurvedic texts describe it as calming and strengthening, used in illness recovery and for older people.

Ayurvedic texts list ashwagandha as one of the main tonics for depletion and weakness. One classical text includes a milk preparation as the origin of the modern ashwagandha latte. Western herbalism adopted the herb through 20th-century stress-support research.

Warm milk preparation (traditional): ½,1 teaspoon of dried root powder simmered in 250 ml whole milk for 5 minutes, sweetened with honey or jaggery if preferred. Taken in the evening. This is the preparation closest to the classical Ayurvedic text.
Herbal extract (dried herb, 1:5 in 40% spirit): steeps 4 to 6 weeks. Dose: 3 to 5 ml in a little water, twice daily. A long-course preparation, take for 6 to 8 weeks then reassess.
Pregnancy: do not use. Ashwagandha has a traditional reputation as a uterine stimulant. Current safety guidance advises against use in pregnancy due to limited safety data.
Autoimmune conditions: take care. Ashwagandha affects immune function. If you have lupus, arthritis, or MS, see a herbalist first. Do not take with ciclosporin, tacrolimus, or methotrexate.

Thyroid: some case reports and trials suggest ashwagandha may affect thyroid hormone levels. If you take levothyroxine or carbimazole, or are being tested for thyroid function, speak to your prescriber before using.
Nightshade family: ashwagandha is a Solanaceae member. In the rare instance of a documented nightshade allergy, avoid.
